run.title: November 2026
run.lineup: crocket 0.5.2, Rocket 0.5.4, Axum 0.8.9, Drogon 1.9.14, Fastify 5.12.8, hyper-express 7.0.2, Spring Boot 3.5.16, and FastAPI 0.165.0
run.lineupShort: crocket against Rocket, Axum, Drogon, Fastify, hyper-express, Spring Boot, and FastAPI

frameworks.name: crocket
frameworks.had: Logger, Metrics, request timeouts, /healthz, /readyz, and x-request-id are built in

frameworks.name: Rocket
frameworks.had: There's no built-in request timeout, and no Prometheus histogram
frameworks.added: rocket_prometheus, a JSON access-log fairing, a request-id fairing, health and ready routes, and a 10 second timeout around the query

frameworks.name: Axum
frameworks.had: These bits aren't built in, though official tower-http layers cover some of them
frameworks.added: a Prometheus histogram, a JSON access-log middleware, tower-http's request-id and 10 second timeout layers, and health and ready routes

frameworks.name: Drogon
frameworks.had: A Prometheus plugin and request advice hooks are available
frameworks.added: a histogram at /metrics, a JSON access log and request-id hook, health and ready routes, and a 10 second database timeout

frameworks.name: Fastify
frameworks.had: pino logging, request-id headers, and timeouts were already there
frameworks.added: prom-client for the histogram, plus health routes and a request-id hook

frameworks.name: hyper-express
frameworks.had: uWebSockets.js underneath gives a body size cap and an idle-connection timeout
frameworks.added: pino for the JSON access log, prom-client for the histogram, a request-id hook, health and ready routes, a hand-written check on POST /echo, a 10 second timeout around the query, and a SIGTERM drain with auto_close off

frameworks.name: Spring Boot
frameworks.added: Actuator and Micrometer for metrics and probes, plus a filter for the request id and the JSON access log

frameworks.name: FastAPI
frameworks.added: prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator for the histogram, asgi-correlation-id for the request id, a JSON access-log and 10 second timeout middleware, and health and ready routes

tests.name: JSON
tests.blurb: Each request encodes {"message":"Hello, World!"} as JSON, and that string is not cached. Same shape as the old TechEmpower JSON test
tests.pendingNote: No results for this test yet
tests.note: This is the HTTP and JSON encoder, no database. Crocket and Drogon stay out in front, and the gap down to Spring Boot and FastAPI is wide

tests.name: Single query
tests.blurb: Each request fetches one random row from a 10,000-row World table and returns it as JSON. Same shape as the old TechEmpower single-query test
tests.pendingNote: No results for this test yet
tests.note: One random row per request. Drogon does come out ahead of crocket here, though it also uses a lot more memory under that load

tests.name: Plaintext
tests.blurb: Each request returns a small Hello, World! text response, which mostly stresses the HTTP pipeline. Same shape as the old TechEmpower plaintext test
tests.pendingNote: No results for this test yet
tests.note: The smallest response, so this is mostly the HTTP pipeline. Crocket's lead is widest here

caveats.text: wrk2 had a 4 vCPU droplet, same size as the app. At crocket's max it was only around half busy (JSON about 50%, plaintext about 55%), so I wouldn't call those numbers client-pegged, though a larger generator could still move them
Drogon does beat crocket on the database test, 49,232 req/s against 45,453, and that's real. It also used about 201 MB of RSS under that load, against 32 MB for crocket

FastAPI tops out around 6,000 req/s on these 4 vCPUs, so at the shared 10,000 (or 4,000 for the query test) requests just queue up. Those wouldn't be fair p50 or p99 figures, which is why the table flags them. The latency you see there is from a rate it can hold, about 60% of its max: 3,500 req/s for JSON, 3,600 for plaintext, and 2,400 for the single query. It ran four uvicorn workers, one per core
Fastify and hyper-express each run as a single Node.js process by default, so they top out around one core. CPU per request is the fairer comparison there
hyper-express grew to about 480 to 780 MB of RSS at max load, though it settled around 232 MB at 3,500 req/s in the soak
Spring Boot needs a one-line property to expose histogram buckets at /metrics, and it's on for every number here

Those wouldn't be fair p50 or p99 figures, which is why the table flags them. The latency you see there is from a rate it can hold, about 60% of its max: 3,500 req/s for JSON, 3,600 for plaintext, and 2,400 for the single query. It ran four uvicorn workers, one per core
notes.coldStart: Cold start is container start to the first 200 on /db. That's the number you feel when a new pod comes up during autoscaling or a deploy. Spring Boot takes about 4–5 seconds here; crocket is around 330 milliseconds

hardwareNote: The JSON, query, and plaintext numbers are from NYC1. The crocket and Drogon production tests ran on the same size in SFO2, because c-4 wasn't available in NYC1 that day. The other production tests, and everything for hyper-express, ran back in NYC1. The graceful drain test ran locally in Docker
